title: One database that runs your team
goal: You will consolidate duplicate task databases into one master database with consistent properties, a project relation, and filtered views.
prerequisites: Two or more Notion databases containing similar tasks
An existing Projects database to relate tasks to
Permission to edit the relevant Notion pages

steps.action: Create a full-page database named Master Tasks.
steps.where: Left sidebar New page button, then the Table database option in the new page.
steps.why: A single source database prevents records and property definitions from drifting apart.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a page titled Master Tasks containing a new table with one blank row.
hint_levels: Start from a new page in the workspace sidebar.
Choose a table that creates a database, not a simple table block.
Click New page, enter Master Tasks, then select Table under Get started with.

steps.action: Add Status, Due, Priority, and Owner properties with matching property types.
steps.where: Master Tasks table header, using the plus button to the right of the existing columns.
steps.why: A shared schema lets every task work with the same filters, sorts, and views.
steps.checkpoint: The table header should show Status, Due, Priority, and Owner columns.
hint_levels: Work across the table's column headers.
Add Status as Status, Due as Date, Priority as Select, and Owner as Person.
Click the header-row + four times; name each property and choose Status, Date, Select, and Person respectively.

steps.action: Add a Project relation property connected to the Projects database.
steps.where: Master Tasks table header plus button, Relation property type, then the database picker.
steps.why: The relation connects each task to its project without duplicating project information.
steps.checkpoint: A Project column should appear, and clicking a cell should offer pages from the Projects database.
hint_levels: Look for the property type that links database pages.
Create a Relation named Project and select the existing Projects database.
Click header-row +, choose Relation, search for and select Projects, click Add relation, then rename the property Project if needed.

steps.action: Move the rows from the first duplicate task database into Master Tasks.
steps.where: Source database table rows and the Move to command in the selected rows menu.
steps.why: Moving pages preserves each task page's content while centralizing its records.
steps.checkpoint: The moved tasks should appear as rows in Master Tasks and no longer appear in the source database.
hint_levels: Select the source rows using their left-edge checkboxes.
Use Move to on the selected pages and choose Master Tasks as the destination.
In the source table, select the rows, open the selected-rows menu, click Move to, search for Master Tasks, and select it.

steps.action: Move the rows from each remaining duplicate task database into Master Tasks.
steps.where: Each source database table, using row checkboxes and the selected rows Move to menu.
steps.why: Completing the migration makes Master Tasks the only task source that needs maintenance.
steps.checkpoint: Master Tasks should contain the tasks from every former duplicate database.
hint_levels: Repeat the same migration for every remaining source.
Select all task rows in each duplicate database and move them to Master Tasks.
Open each source database, select its rows, choose Move to, and select Master Tasks.

steps.action: Fill any blank Status, Due, Priority, Owner, and Project cells for the imported tasks.
steps.where: Master Tasks table cells under the corresponding property columns.
steps.why: Complete properties make the upcoming views accurate and useful.
steps.checkpoint: Every imported row should have a Status and Project, with other known values visible in their columns.
hint_levels: Scan for empty cells across the shared properties.
Click empty cells and choose or enter the correct value for each imported task.
In Master Tasks, click each blank property cell and select its Status, date, Priority, Owner, or related Project page.

steps.action: Create a linked view of Master Tasks on the page where you want a focused task list.
steps.where: Target Notion page body, slash-command menu, Linked view of database option.
steps.why: A linked view shows a tailored slice of the master data without creating duplicate records.
steps.checkpoint: The target page should display a database view whose source is Master Tasks.
hint_levels: Add a database view inside the destination page.
Choose a linked database view and connect it to Master Tasks.
On the target page, type /linked, select Linked view of database, search for Master Tasks, and select it.

steps.action: Filter the linked view to show only unfinished tasks for one project.
steps.where: Linked database toolbar, Filter button, advanced filter menu.
steps.why: Filters replace separate project databases while keeping every task in the master source.
steps.checkpoint: The view should show only rows for the chosen project whose Status is not Done.
hint_levels: Use both the Project and Status properties to narrow the view.
Add Project contains your chosen project and Status is not Done.
Click Filter, add Project → contains → select the project, then add Status → is not → Done.

steps.action: Create a second view grouped by Status and sorted by Due date.
steps.where: View name dropdown at the upper-left of the linked database, New view command, then Group and Sort toolbar controls.
steps.why: Multiple views provide different workflows over the same underlying records.
steps.checkpoint: A second view tab should be visible with Status groups and earlier due dates listed first.
hint_levels: Create another perspective from the view switcher.
Add a new view, group it by Status, and sort Due ascending.
Click the current view name, click New view, name it Workflow, click Create, then choose Group → Status and Sort → Due → Ascending.
